name: So You're C-Tier Now: A Practical Guide to Not Dying in Your First Month
author: Anonymous (attributed to Twice-Dead Malika in Signal Network circles)
description: A practical survival guide circulated through the Gray Zone district drop points and broker waiting rooms across GLMZ, attributed by reputation to a freelancer known as Twice-Dead Malika — the name itself a reference to two confirmed flatlines and subsequent resuscitations during early career jobs. The guide is typeset in a compressed sans-serif and appears to have been photocopied from a photocopied original, with margin notes in at least three different hands in later editions. It is addressed directly to new C-tier freelancers with no patience for sentimentality and a specific focus on the logistical, financial, and social failures that kill new entrants before combat ever gets the chance.
body:
You are C-tier. That means the Signal Network knows you exist and has decided not to warn people away from you yet. That's it. That's the whole achievement. Don't frame it on your wall.

Most C-tiers die in the first thirty days. Not from bullets. From bad math, bad water, and misreading a broker's smile. This guide exists because someone should have handed it to me before I needed a crash cart twice.

---

**READING A POSTING WITHOUT GETTING KILLED BY IT**

A posting has three things that matter: the stated objective, the listed hazard tier, and who's paying.

Ignore the payout number until you've looked at all three. A Φ400 courier job in a Narrows transit zone is not the same as a Φ400 courier job in the Gray Zone Block 9 during a Arcturus sweep cycle. Same number. One of them you probably survive. Learn to read what the posting isn't saying.

Hazard tiers in postings are self-reported by the broker. There is no regulatory body. "Low hazard" means the broker doesn't want to pay hazard premium, not that it's actually low hazard. When a posting says Low Hazard and the location is anywhere in the Gray Zone below Level 14, someone is lying to you or to themselves.

Who's paying matters more than how much. A Φ600 first job from an unvetted poster with no broker intermediary is a trap or a test or both. If you can't find a single dead drop token in the network that vouches for the posting origin, walk away. Φ600 doesn't help you if you're being used as a disposable asset for something the actual client doesn't want traced.

Realistic first-job range: Φ80 to Φ250 for legitimate C-tier work. Anyone offering you significantly more than that before you have a single completed job in your chain either doesn't know what they're doing or does know what they're doing and you're the one who's going to find out.

---

**GEAR THAT MATTERS VS. GEAR THAT'S MARKETING**

You have maybe Φ300 total after whatever it cost you to get here. Here's what you actually need:

Footwear. Waterproof, ankle-support, resoleable. Spend Φ60-80 here. You will walk more than you will fight. Your feet are your logistics chain. The number of C-tiers I watched limp off a job with split soles and then miss their next posting because they couldn't move — I stopped counting.

Water filtration. Personal, pocketable, Φ15-25 at any the Gray Zone hardware drop. GLMZ infrastructure water in the Gray Zone is not reliable. The Narrows is inconsistent. Extended jobs — anything over six hours in-zone — require you to source water locally. "I didn't have clean water" is the cause of death on more C-tier incident reports than firearms.

A knife. Not a combat knife. A tool. Φ20-40. It opens things, cuts things, fixes things, and yes, occasionally it's the last option you have. But you are buying it for the first three uses.

Basic medical. Wound seal, broad-spectrum antibiotic tabs, two doses of stimulant for emergencies. Total: Φ40-60 if you know where to source it. the Gray Zone has a dozen gray-market medic suppliers; any broker who won't tell you where the nearest one is either doesn't care if you live or is testing your resourcefulness. Either way, find it yourself.

Communication. If you don't have a BCI — and a lot of the Gray Zone-borns don't — you need a hardened short-range comm unit. Φ30-50, secondhand. Non-negotiable. You cannot complete jobs reliably without being able to confirm handoffs and signal abort.

What you do not need: tactical vest rigs (Φ200+ and marks you as a target in transit), any weapon that requires charging infrastructure you don't control, neural overlay packages marketed to "new freelancers" (they are surveillance tools that pay you a Φ10 signup bonus and sell your behavioral data to broker aggregators), and anything described in a posting as "provided equipment" that you don't get to inspect beforehand.

---

**HOW TO READ A BROKER**

Brokers who are good for C-tier work are not the same as brokers who are good, full stop. A broker with an A-tier reputation who doesn't work with C-tiers is useless to you and may actively resent the interaction.

What you want: a broker who has completed transactions with at least three C-tiers who survived and moved up. Ask other C-tiers. Ask them in person. Dead drops in the Gray Zone transit corridors, not in digital spaces that can be monitored.

Signs a broker is reliable: they tell you when a job is above your current capability. This costs them a commission. A broker who turns down the fee to keep you from getting killed is a broker who wants you to become B-tier and bring them more business. Self-interest that aligns with your survival is the closest thing to trust you're going to find at this level.

Signs a broker is not reliable: they have a very clean office. Seriously. A the Gray Zone-district broker with expensive lighting and a proper desk either has money from sources that aren't completion fees, or they're moving up-market and you're filler work to them. Reliable C-tier brokers operate out of transit alcoves, repair shops, the back thirds of Narrows canteens.

Never pay a broker upfront. A broker who asks for a "registration fee" or "signal access fee" before your first job is taking Φ40 from fifty new C-tiers a month and has no intention of posting you anything real. This is a known racket. You will feel stupid when it happens to you. Everyone does. Don't let it happen twice.

---

**HOW YOU ACTUALLY DIE: THE REAL LIST**

1. Dehydration and heat exhaustion on extended jobs. Already covered. Carry water. Find water. Make this a reflex.

2. Overconfidence after your first completed job. You survived once. Your brain will interpret this as evidence that you know what you're doing. You don't yet. The second job is statistically more dangerous than the first because you stop treating it like it might kill you.

3. Bad intel accepted without verification. Someone tells you a transit corridor is clear. You take their word for it. It wasn't clear. Verify what you can verify. Ask where the information came from. If nobody knows, that's your answer.

4. Debt. Taking a job because you owe someone. Owed money creates bad decision-making faster than anything except maybe grief. Do not borrow from anyone connected to the broker ecosystem in your first thirty days. The interest structures are not legal because there is no legal. They are enforced.

5. Isolation. Working alone because you don't trust anyone yet. Valid instinct, wrong application. Find one other C-tier you can verify through even a single shared vouch. Not a partner — a contact. Someone who knows where you're going and will notice if you don't come back. This has saved my life more than any piece of gear.

---

**BUILDING YOUR FIRST VOUCH CHAIN**

Complete a job. Ask the broker to leave a token. They will usually do this if the job went clean — it costs them nothing and a vouched C-tier is worth more to them than an unvouched one. That's one token.

Find where tokens aggregate in your zone. Ask a C-tier who's been around longer than you. Buy them something to eat first. This is not bribery, it's establishing that you are a person who understands how exchange works.

You do not need many vouches to move. You need legible ones. Two tokens from brokers anyone has heard of beats six tokens from sources nobody can trace. Quality of chain matters more than length.

Do not vouch for anyone you have not personally worked alongside. Your vouch is your reputation extended. A new C-tier who asks you for a vouch after one conversation is asking you to risk your chain on a stranger. Say no. They'll understand or they'll be angry and either way you made the right call.

---

**WHAT NOT TO SPEND YOUR FIRST PAYOUT ON**

Augmentation. I know. I know what it feels like to watch chrome-limbed B-tiers move through a job like the physics are different for them. They are not wrong. But Φ200 from a first job does not buy you good augmentation. It buys you gray-market chrome that will get infected, malfunction under load, or be slaved to a payment plan with terms that are not in your favor. Save. Stack jobs. Buy it right or buy it never.

Celebration. One meal. One drink. That's the rule. You earned it. You also need the rest of it to survive the next thirty days.

Trust. You cannot buy it and you cannot rush it. It accumulates from showing up, doing the work, not lying about what you can do, and being the person who noticed when someone needed water at hour seven of a job.

You're C-tier. That's the beginning of something, not the end of something.

Most of you will not read this carefully enough. Some of you will read it and die anyway because the world doesn't grade on effort. A few of you will still be working in two years and you'll recognize everything in here from the inside.

I hope you're in that last group. I have no way to know.

— M.
